items.alt: Looking down into an indigo vat: dark blue-green liquid with a coppery bloom gathered to one side
items.description: Natural indigo, fructose, calcium hydroxide, a thermometer and the same one-page method sheet that is pinned above our own vat. It makes a five-litre vat that will keep going for a month if you feed it.
items.name: Indigo kit for one vat
items.summary: Enough to dye about two kilos, and the instructions we use.

items.alt: Five hanks of yarn hanging from a rail, dyed weld yellow, madder red, indigo, cochineal pink and walnut brown
items.description: Wool takes indigo faster than plant fibre and gives it back faster too. Four dips is what we have found holds through a wash without going stiff.
items.name: Indigo yarn, worsted

items.alt: A square of linen dyed with walnut husk, warm brown
items.description: Walnut is a substantive dye: it needs no mordant, which means the whole process is husks, water and time. The husks come from a single tree and the quantity is whatever that tree drops.
items.lead_time: Cut and sent within two days.
items.name: Walnut hemp
items.summary: Husks from one tree in Wiltshire. No mordant, no waste.

items.alt: A square of linen dyed with logwood, dusty purple
items.description: Logwood makes a purple nothing else does and it is not light fast: hang this in a south window and it will be grey-brown in a year. Line a coat with it and it will outlive the coat.
items.lead_time: Three weeks, dyed to your length.
items.name: Logwood wool
items.summary: A purple that fades, honestly labelled.

items.alt: A square of linen dyed indigo, the weave and the unevenness of the bath both visible
items.description: Belgian flax, woven in Somerset at 300 grams, then dipped eight times over two days. The colour sits on the surface of the fibre rather than in it, which is why indigo wears the way it does: it goes lighter where you use it and keeps the rest.
items.lead_time: Cut and sent within two days.
items.name: Indigo linen, heavy
items.summary: Eight dips. The blue that keeps its green in the shade.

items.alt: A square of linen dyed madder red
items.description: Madder root gives everything from apricot to brick depending on how hard the water is and how patient you are. This is the patient end: two hours held under a simmer it never reaches.
items.lead_time: Cut and sent within two days.
items.name: Madder linen
items.summary: Three years in the ground, one afternoon in the pot.

items.alt: A square of linen dyed weld yellow
items.description: Weld was grown for this and almost nothing else. It is a clean yellow with none of the green that turmeric brings, and unlike turmeric it stays.
items.lead_time: Next bath is the first week of October.
items.name: Weld cotton
items.summary: The oldest yellow in Europe, on a cloth you can push a needle through.

items.alt: A square of linen dyed cochineal, deep pink
items.description: Cochineal is an insect dye and there is no way to say that nicely, so we say it plainly: about twelve grams of dried cochineal goes into a metre of this. If that is not for you, the madder is the closest red we have.
items.lead_time: Back in November, if the bath goes well.
items.name: Cochineal silk
items.summary: Twelve grams of insect for a metre of cloth. We say so.
